title: Compiler and Language Toolchain Database — Overview and definition
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Languages, compilers, interpreters, build systems, and compatibility information. The Compiler and Language Toolchain Database documents the machinery that turns source code into running programs: languages with their paradigms and type systems, compilers and interpreters with their flags and behaviors, build systems with their dependency models, and the compatibility matrix between them. 'It compiles on my machine' fails when toolchains differ — this database records exactly which toolchain builds what, so builds are portable by construction.

title: Compiler and Language Toolchain Database — Knowledge: technical reference
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Pipeline: source -> frontend (lex, parse, type-check -> IR) -> optimizer (middle-end passes on IR) -> backend (instruction selection, register allocation, codegen). Interpreters skip codegen and execute AST/bytecode directly. Key concepts: optimization levels (-O0 debug, -O2 balanced, -O3 aggressive, -Os size); undefined behavior (the compiler may assume it never happens — the classic C/C++ trap); ABI compatibility (name mangling, calling conventions, struct layout); build systems: explicit (Make), generated (CMake), hermetic (Bazel: sandboxed, content-addressed). Diagnostics: warnings are the compiler telling you about probable bugs — warning sets per compiler recorded. Reproducible builds: same inputs -> same bytes (timestamps and paths normalized).

title: Compiler and Language Toolchain Database — Verification: tests and limitations
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Tests: recommendation test (known-good combos recommended); translation test (flag mappings verified against compiler docs); diagnostic test (sample errors map to correct fixes); determinism test. Limitations: new compiler releases change behavior — recheck; cross-compilation needs target sysroots; proprietary toolchains have thinner records. Every record names exact versions.
